title: Possessive suffixes
topic: סִפְרִי, בֵּיתֵנוּ, אִשְׁתּוֹ: the formal possessive
why: The formal possessive, attached to the noun (sifri, beitenu, ishto), which you'll meet in writing and in set phrases like "in my opinion" or "my husband." It builds on the smikhut and prepares you to read more polished texts.

{"lessons": ["

Two ways to say \"my\"

You know הַסֵּפֶר שֶׁלִּי: it's the everyday way, in speech as well as in writing. Hebrew has a second, more formal way: attaching the possessive to the end of the noun, a bit as if English said \"book-my.\"

הַסֵּפֶר שֶׁלִּי = סִפְרִיmy book [ha-sefer sheli = sifri]
Whose?bookhouse
myסִפְרִי sifriבֵּיתִי beiti
your (m.)סִפְרְךָ sifrekhaבֵּיתְךָ beitkha
your (f.)סִפְרֵךְ sifrekhבֵּיתֵךְ beitekh
hisסִפְרוֹ sifroבֵּיתוֹ beito
herסִפְרָהּ sifraבֵּיתָהּ beita
ourסִפְרֵנוּ sifrenuבֵּיתֵנוּ beitenu
your (pl. m.)סִפְרְכֶם sifrekhemבֵּיתְכֶם beitkhem
theirסִפְרָם siframבֵּיתָם beitam

The endings look like those of לִי, לוֹ, לָהּ, לָנוּ: i = my, o = his, a with a dot in the הּ = her, enu = our, am = their. Like English, Hebrew tells \"his\" and \"her\" apart.

The noun often changes a little, as in smikhut: סֵפֶר becomes סִפְר־, בַּיִת becomes בֵּית־, as in בֵּית סֵפֶר.

", "

Feminine nouns: ה becomes ת

As in smikhut (שָׂפָה → שְׂפַת), the final ה of a feminine noun becomes ת before the suffix:

Nounmyhisour
מִשְׁפָּחָה familyמִשְׁפַּחְתִּי mishpakhtiמִשְׁפַּחְתּוֹ mishpakhtoמִשְׁפַּחְתֵּנוּ mishpakhtenu
דִּירָה apartmentדִּירָתִי diratiדִּירָתוֹ diratoדִּירָתֵנוּ diratenu
עֲבוֹדָה work, jobעֲבוֹדָתִי avodatiעֲבוֹדָתוֹ avodatoעֲבוֹדָתֵנוּ avodatenu

Family words are a bit irregular, but very common: אִשְׁתִּי (my wife), בַּעֲלִי (my husband), אָחִי (my brother), אֲחוֹתִי (my sister), בְּנִי (my son), בִּתִּי (my daughter).

אִשְׁתּוֹ עוֹבֶדֶת בְּבֵית חוֹלִים, וּבְנָם לוֹמֵד בָּאוּנִיבֶרְסִיטָה.His wife works in a hospital, and their son is studying at the university. [ishto ovedet be-veit kholim, u-vnam lomed ba-universita.]

The trap: אִשָּׁה becomes אִשְׁתּ־, not \"ishat-\": אִשְׁתִּי [ishti], אִשְׁתּוֹ [ishto].

", "

In real life

In speech, Israelis mostly say הַבַּיִת שֶׁלִּי. The suffixes are kept for polished writing (letters, articles, speeches) and for set phrases everyone uses:

  • שְׁמִי…: my name is… (a bit formal; in speech, קוֹרְאִים לִי…)
  • בַּעֲלִי, אִשְׁתִּי: very common in speech too
  • לְדַעְתִּי (in my opinion), לְצַעֲרִי (unfortunately, lit. \"to my regret\")
  • אָחִי: my brother… and, in slang, \"bro\"

Two rules: no article on a noun with a suffix (you say סִפְרִי, without הַ), but the adjective that follows takes the article: סִפְרִי הֶחָדָשׁ (my new book), בֵּיתֵנוּ הַגָּדוֹל (our big house).

In the plural, a י appears before the suffix: חֲבֵרַי (my friends), יְלָדֵינוּ (our children). For now, just learn to recognize them.
